form.label: Foundational Workshop 2 - What You Built
form.description: Capstone dashboard for Foundational Workshop #2: Petclinic request traffic, OTTL-derived severity, and the log-to-two-indexes routing pattern.

div.p: You wired up multiline stack-trace parsing, added an OTTL transform to derive log severity, and routed one Kubernetes log stream into two indexes via a pod annotation — this dashboard is the proof, built entirely from the data you generated.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs http_status=* | stats count as value | table value
index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs http_status=* | stats count as total count(eval(http_status>=500)) as errors | eval value=round((errors/total)*100,1) | table value
index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs http_status=* | rex field=http_path mode=sed "s/;jsessionid=[A-F0-9]+//" | rex field=http_path mode=sed "s|/[0-9]+|/{id}|g" | stats dc(http_path) as value | table value

panel.title: Request Volume Over Time (5xx vs. Everything Else)

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs http_status=* | eval status_class=if(http_status>=500,"5xx (error)","Other") | timechart span=$span_token$ count by status_class

panel.title: Severity / Status Breakdown — Powered by the OTTL Severity Transform

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs | stats count by http_status "otel.log.severity.text" | sort -count

panel.title: Most Recent Errors — RuntimeException Stack Traces (Multiline Parsing in Action)

search.query: index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs RuntimeException | sort -_time | head 15 | table _time severity trace_id "service.name"

panel.title: Index Routing Proof — One Log Stream Becomes Two (via the Pod Annotation)

search.query: (index=k8s_ws_logs OR index=k8s_ws_petclinic_logs) | stats count by index sourcetype | sort -count

div.h2: What This Data Lets You Answer — The Kubernetes Audit Log
div.p: Everything above proves your pipeline works. Everything below shows why it was worth building. The same Collector that shipped your application logs is also shipping the kube-apiserver audit stream — a record of every call made to your cluster's control plane: who made it, what they touched, whether it was allowed.

No application log can answer “who deleted that deployment?” or “is anything unauthenticated talking to my API server?” These panels can. On this lab cluster the answers are reassuringly boring — that is the point: these are the exact queries whose non-boring answers matter in production.

panel.title: Who Is Talking to Your Kubernetes API — Top Identities by Verb
panel.description: Every bar is an identity that authenticated (or didn't) to your control plane, split by what it asked for. Conclude: a healthy cluster is dominated by its own machinery - controllers, the scheduler, kubelet, and your Collector's service account - all doing predictable read/watch work. The identity to look for in production is the one you cannot name: a human user or service account you didn't provision, or a known account suddenly issuing verbs it never used before.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_logs sourcetype="kube:container:kube-apiserver" verb=* | eval identity='user.username' | chart useother=f count over identity by verb | addtotals fieldname=Total | sort -Total | head 10 | fields - Total

panel.title: Unauthenticated (Anonymous) API Access Over Time
panel.description: Requests reaching the API server with no credentials, as system:anonymous. Conclude: a flat, metronomic line like this one is health probing, not an attack - kubelet and the load balancer poll /readyz and /livez on a fixed interval, so the shape is a constant. What you are watching for in production is the shape changing: a step up, a burst, or anonymous traffic appearing at a time of day when nothing should be probing. This is the panel that turns "we collect audit logs" into "we would notice."

search.query: index=k8s_ws_logs sourcetype="kube:container:kube-apiserver" "user.username"="system:anonymous" | timechart span=$span_token$ useother=f limit=8 count by requestURI

panel.title: … And What That Anonymous Caller Is Actually Hitting
panel.description: The same unauthenticated traffic, resolved to endpoint, client, and source IP. Conclude: this is benign - kube-probe and a Go HTTP client issuing GET against the three health endpoints from inside the cluster network, which is exactly what Kubernetes is designed to allow without credentials. Judge a real cluster the same way, on three questions: is the URI a health endpoint or a real resource path, is the user agent a known probe or a scanner, and is the source IP inside your network. An anonymous GET against /api/v1/namespaces/default/secrets from an unfamiliar IP is the same query returning a very different answer.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_logs sourcetype="kube:container:kube-apiserver" "user.username"="system:anonymous" | stats count as Requests values("sourceIPs{}") as "Source IP" values(verb) as Verbs by requestURI userAgent | rename requestURI as "Request URI" userAgent as "User Agent" | sort -Requests | table "Request URI" "User Agent" "Source IP" Verbs Requests

panel.title: API Operation Mix — Which Verbs Against Which Resources
panel.description: The shape of normal control-plane chatter. Conclude: watch and update against endpoints, endpointslices, and leases should dominate - that is service discovery and leader election keeping themselves alive, and it is load-bearing noise, not waste. Read this panel as a baseline you now own. The deviations that matter later are create or delete appearing on pods outside a deploy window, any get against secrets, or a single resource suddenly outweighing the leases traffic.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_logs sourcetype="kube:container:kube-apiserver" verb=* "objectRef.resource"=* | eval resource='objectRef.resource' | chart useother=f count over resource by verb | addtotals fieldname=Total | sort -Total | head 12 | fields - Total

panel.title: Write Operations Audit Trail — Who Changed What
panel.description: Mutating verbs only: create, update, patch, delete. Conclude: on an idle cluster this list is short and entirely machine-driven - the storage provisioner refreshing endpoints, the kubelet and API server renewing their leases, a node status patch. Every row is an identity, an action, an object, and a timestamp, which is the whole compliance answer to "who changed this, and when." The row that should stop you in production is one whose user.username is a person or an unexpected service account, especially on delete.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_logs sourcetype="kube:container:kube-apiserver" (verb=create OR verb=update OR verb=patch OR verb=delete) | stats count as Operations values("objectRef.namespace") as Namespace latest(_time) as last_seen by "user.username" verb "objectRef.resource" | eval "Last Seen"=strftime(last_seen,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S") | rename "user.username" as Identity verb as Verb "objectRef.resource" as Resource | sort -Operations | head 20 | table Identity Verb Resource Namespace Operations "Last Seen"

panel.title: Sensitive Resource Access — Secrets, Service Accounts, and RBAC
panel.description: Every touch of the objects that grant access: secrets, serviceaccounts, roles, rolebindings, and their cluster-scoped equivalents, plus configmaps. Conclude: legitimate access here is almost entirely watch by system:apiserver, the controller manager, and the scheduler - they must observe these objects to function. The signals to alert on are different verbs and different actors: a get or list against secrets (that is a read of the actual value), or any create or patch of a rolebinding, which is how an attacker turns a foothold into cluster-admin.

search.query: index=k8s_ws_logs sourcetype="kube:container:kube-apiserver" ("objectRef.resource"=secrets OR "objectRef.resource"=configmaps OR "objectRef.resource"=serviceaccounts OR "objectRef.resource"=roles OR "objectRef.resource"=rolebindings OR "objectRef.resource"=clusterroles OR "objectRef.resource"=clusterrolebindings) | stats count as Requests by "objectRef.resource" verb "user.username" | rename "objectRef.resource" as Resource verb as Verb "user.username" as Identity | sort -Requests | head 20 | table Resource Verb Identity Requests
